newsitem.title: USA: Florida governor steps into Miami budget crisis.
newsitem.headline: Florida governor steps into Miami budget crisis.

text.p: Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles sent top aides to meet Miami's city manager on Tuesday amid reports a state takeover of the financially strapped city was imminent.

The meeting with City Manager Ed Marquez was set for 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT) in Miami, Marquez's secretary said. Chiles scheduled a news conference in Tallahassee at 3:30 p.m. EST (2030 GMT) to discuss the situation.
While state and city officials wrangled with Miami's $68 million deficit, city inspectors fanned out in search of scofflaws who owe an estimated $1 million in unpaid garbage collection fees.
The Miami Herald reported Tuesday that the city was uncertain how many garbage customers it serves and how many accounts may be delinquent.
In some instances, property owners illegally built additions to homes, which were rented to people who do not pay for garbage pickup.

But Joseph Ruiz Jr., a Dade County solid waste official loaned temporarily to the city, said Miami's solid waste division had no method of checking the number of homes served against the number of bills paid.
"Something is wrong with this picture," Ruiz told the newspaper.
The disorganization in the solid waste department underscores the fiscal chaos uncovered after the former city manager and former finance director resigned to face federal corruption charges.
An interim city manager discovered the deficit in Miami's $275 million budget for the year that began Oct. 1, and said the city was owed millions in unpaid rents and fees.
Last week Mayor Joe Carollo officially notified the governor that the city had a financial crisis and said he would welcome the appointment of a state emergency board to run the city.
Miami made a $10.8 million payment on its bonds Monday, leaving it with $45 million in cash. Revenue from property tax payments should keep the city operating until late February or March.
"But unless they do something, obviously the money will run out," said John Incorvaia, vice president for municipal finance at Moody's Investor's Service Inc.

Last month the state advanced the city $22 million in sales tax revenues that otherwise would have been paid over six months. Chiles has since criticised the city for failing to act quickly enough to raise garbage fees and take other steps to close the budget gap permanently.
State officials told Moody's "they will imminently declare the City of Miami to be in a state of "Financial Emergency."
That would allow the governor to appoint a financial emergencies board to take over city finances.
Although city officials have introduced the possibility of filing for bankruptcy under Chapter 9, they could not do that without the governor's permisson.
